strengths: Timely and practically relevant focus on evaluating how modern compression methods (quantization, distillation, and pruning) affect large reasoning models (LRMs) like DeepSeek-R1.
Comprehensive coverage of different compression paradigms across diverse reasoning categories (mathematical, logical, temporal, and multihop).
Detailed analysis of model collapse points across varying pruning sparsity ratios.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: The paper does not propose new algorithms, architectures, or compression methodologies. Instead, it runs off-the-shelf tools and checkpoints (Unsloth GGUF models, official DeepSeek distillations, and SparseGPT) on existing benchmark tasks.

Small evaluation scale and lack of statistical rigor: AIME 2024 contains only 30 questions, meaning a difference of a single question changes accuracy by 3.33%. MuSiQue is evaluated on only 100 sampled questions. Furthermore, inference is performed with temperature 0.6 in a single pass without reporting variance, multiple seeds, or error bars.

Flawed causal interpretation of test-time compute: In Section 5.4, the finding that shorter outputs achieve higher accuracy than longer outputs is largely confounded by problem difficulty. Harder problems naturally trigger extended reasoning, backtracking, and eventual failure, whereas easier problems can be solved directly in fewer tokens. Post-hoc splitting into shortest vs. longest buckets does not isolate verbosity as the root cause of errors.

Absence of computational and efficiency metrics: For a paper centered on model compression, there is no empirical profiling of memory consumption, token generation throughput, latency, or actual hardware speedup across the tested configurations.

Predictable pruning collapse behavior: Unstructured one-shot pruning of LLMs beyond 50–60% sparsity without retraining or fine-tuning is well documented in prior literature to cause degeneration and repetition loops; the paper's findings in this regard offer little new insight.

strengths: Timely and practically relevant focus on the compression characteristics (quantization, distillation, and pruning) of open-source Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) such as DeepSeek-R1.

Comprehensive coverage of three major model compression paradigms, evaluating dynamic sub-2-bit quantization, distilled dense architectures (LLaMA-70B and Qwen-32B backbones), and post-training unstructured pruning across multiple sparsity levels.
Interesting observations regarding failure modes under heavy pruning, specifically documenting repetitive degeneration patterns and benchmark-dependent collapse points.
weaknesses: Limited evaluation scale and benchmark coverage: AIME 2024 contains only 30 questions, where a difference of 1-2 problems causes substantial variance (3.3% per problem), and MuSiQue is evaluated on only a 100-sample subset. Standard reasoning benchmarks widely used in the LRM literature (e.g., MATH-500, GPQA Diamond, Codeforces/LiveCodeBench) are missing, limiting the generality of the empirical claims.

Methodological flaw in the test-time compute analysis: Comparing post-hoc the accuracy of the shortest 20–30% versus longest 20–30% of outputs conflates correlation with causation. Inherently easier problems naturally require fewer reasoning steps, whereas difficult problems trigger extensive search, backtracking, or failure loops. Concluding that 'shorter outputs generally achieve better performance... highlighting the need to reduce verbosity' is an artifact of problem difficulty selection bias rather than controlled evidence that verbosity degrades reasoning.

Approximation shortcuts in measurement: Rather than using the model family's native BPE tokenizers to measure test-time compute, the study merely treats whitespace-delimited words as tokens ('treat words within each output as tokens for simplicity'), which is imprecise for code, mathematical notation, and multilingual tokens.

Conflated pruning setup: Due to tooling constraints on 671B MoE architectures, pruning is performed exclusively on the already-distilled models (R1-Distill-Llama-70B and R1-Distill-Qwen-32B). As a result, the paper does not actually evaluate pruning on DeepSeek-R1 itself, but rather compound compression (distillation + pruning) on standard dense models.

Lack of technical novelty: The paper does not propose new compression algorithms, quantization schemes, or reasoning-aware pruning objectives; it serves purely as an empirical benchmarking study, but without the statistical rigor, sample size, or controlled counterfactuals expected of a standalone benchmarking contribution at a top-tier venue.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and practically relevant topic: evaluating how post-training compression techniques (quantization, distillation, and pruning) impact large reasoning models (LRMs) such as DeepSeek-R1.
The empirical sweep over pruning sparsity levels (from 10% to 80% on the distilled models) provides a clear view of degradation thresholds across different task types.
The paper is clearly structured, easy to read, and well-organized.
weaknesses: Limited novelty and technical contribution: The work does not introduce novel compression algorithms, architectures, or evaluation metrics. It evaluates existing artifacts (Unsloth quantized weights, DeepSeek open weights) and applies standard off-the-shelf SparseGPT to distilled checkpoints.

Small sample sizes and lack of statistical rigor: The evaluation uses very small sample sets (e.g., only 30 questions for AIME 2024 and only 100 sampled questions for MuSiQue). With non-zero sampling temperature (T=0.6, top_p=0.95), results from a single run are subject to substantial variance, yet no standard deviations, confidence intervals, or multiple runs are provided.

Absence of efficiency and deployment metrics: For an empirical study on model compression, omitting actual hardware profiling—such as GPU memory footprint, tokens-per-second throughput, and latency speedups—severely limits the practical utility of the findings.

Confounded analysis of test-time compute: The observation that shorter responses achieve higher accuracy than longer ones conflates problem difficulty with reasoning verbosity. On harder problems, reasoning models naturally spend more tokens exploring hypotheses and backtracking, or degenerate into repetition loops when failing. Post-hoc splitting into shortest vs. longest does not establish that reducing verbosity improves reasoning performance.

Questionable setup for knowledge vs. reasoning claims: Drawing strong claims that parameter count impacts knowledge memorization more than reasoning capability based entirely on a 100-sample closed-book evaluation of MuSiQue (a benchmark designed for multi-hop reading comprehension/retrieval) is methodologically weak, as performance is near floor level (1-17% EM).

strengths: Timely and relevant topic: With the emergence of large reasoning models (LRMs) like DeepSeek-R1, understanding how compression (quantization, pruning, distillation) affects reasoning capabilities versus parametric knowledge is crucial.

Combination of mechanistic interpretability and compression: The adaptation of difference-of-means steering vectors and attribution patching to study module-level sensitivity across specific reasoning behaviors (backtracking, uncertainty estimation, example testing, adding knowledge) is an engaging and promising analytical framework.

Actionable validation: The authors validate their interpretability findings both negatively (quantizing only the identified critical module `32_up` causes a large performance drop in Table 3) and positively (protecting the final-layer MLP modules in FP16 yields significant accuracy recovery in 3-bit AWQ in Table 4).
weaknesses: Limited benchmark size and scope: The evaluation relies on very small test sets. AIME 2024 contains only 30 problems (meaning a single problem accounts for ~3.33% accuracy), and MuSiQue is evaluated on a random subsample of only 100 problems. Including larger, standard reasoning benchmarks (such as MATH-500, GPQA-Diamond, or GSM8K) would make the empirical findings much more robust against statistical noise.

Overstated novelty regarding layer sensitivity: It is well-documented in existing post-training quantization literature (e.g., AWQ, SpQR, SqueezeLLM, SmoothQuant) that the first and last layers of Transformer LLMs are highly sensitive to quantization and typically benefit from being kept in higher precision (e.g., FP16). The paper frames the importance of final-layer modules as a brand-new discovery rather than properly situating it in the context of established mixed-precision practices.

Details and validation of behavioral annotations: The extraction of the four reasoning behaviors relies on prompting GPT-4o to segment model outputs. The paper lacks analysis on annotation quality, inter-annotator agreement, or how robust the resulting steering vectors and importance attributions are to variations in this prompting pipeline.

Presentation and execution issues: There are several signs of rushed writing, including a cut-off sentence in Footnote 1 ('Our interpretation code is a'), an apparent typo in the Figure 5 caption ('Change of $RI_{m\ell}^c$ from DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B to Qwen2.5-Math-7B'), and spelling mistakes in the conclusion ('imrpving').

strengths: Timely and practically important focus on understanding how compression techniques (quantization, distillation, pruning) impact large reasoning models (LRMs) like DeepSeek-R1 and its distilled variants.

Combines broad empirical benchmarking with mechanistic interpretability (difference of means and attribution patching) to locate critical weights and explain failure modes of compression on specific reasoning behaviors (backtracking, uncertainty estimation, etc.).

Provides actionable and validated insights: identifying that the final-layer MLP (particularly `up_proj` and `gate_proj`) is critical and disproportionately degraded by quantization, and demonstrating that a lightweight mixed-precision strategy protecting ~2% of weights in FP16 significantly recovers 3-bit quantization performance.
Comprehensive benchmarking across multiple model scales (7B to 671B), model families (Llama, Qwen, DeepSeek), and quantization/pruning techniques (AWQ, GPTQ, GPTAQ, ANY4/3, SparseGPT).
weaknesses: Missing critical control baselines for the selective protection experiment in Table 4: The paper demonstrates that keeping the final-layer MLP in FP16 improves 3-bit AWQ performance, but does not benchmark against protecting other layers (e.g., first layer, middle layers, or random layers) with an equivalent parameter budget to prove that this benefit is uniquely attributable to the final layer.

The evaluation on knowledge retention relies solely on a small subset of 100 samples from MuSiQue. Making the sweeping claim that weight count affects knowledge memorization more than reasoning based on such a small sample on a multi-hop QA task is statistically weak and insufficiently supported compared to standard knowledge benchmarks (e.g., TriviaQA, PopQA, or MMLU).

Mechanistic interpretability analysis is restricted to small distilled models (7B/8B). It remains unverified whether the specific localization patterns (e.g., final-layer MLP importance) transfer to the full Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) 671B DeepSeek-R1 architecture.

Drafting oversights and errors: Footnote 1 on page 2 is truncated ('Our interpretation code is a'); there is a typo in Section 6 ('imrpving'); and Figure 5 caption incorrectly mixes model families ('from DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B to Qwen2.5-Math-7B (the backbone model)').

strengths: Timely and relevant topic: understanding how model compression (quantization, distillation, and pruning) affects the reasoning behavior of Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) such as DeepSeek-R1 and its distilled variants is of significant practical interest.

Comprehensive coverage of compression paradigms: the authors benchmark multiple post-training quantization methods (AWQ, GPTQ, GPTAQ, ANY4/3, dynamic quantization), distillation checkpoints, and unstructured pruning (SparseGPT).

Application of mechanistic interpretability: adapting difference of means and attribution patching to analyze linear module importance across distinct reasoning behaviors (e.g., backtracking, uncertainty estimation) provides an interesting analytical angle.
weaknesses: Small sample sizes and limited benchmark scale: Several key conclusions rely on very small test sets. AIME 2024 contains only 30 problems (meaning a single correct answer changes accuracy by 3.33%), and MuSiQue is evaluated on a sampled subset of only 100 questions. This small sample size introduces high variance and limits the statistical reliability of the reported collapse points and comparisons.

Conflation of base model capacity with distillation effects in knowledge retention claims: The claim that 'distillation and pruning compress knowledge retention more than reasoning capabilities' is drawn primarily from closed-book evaluation on 100 MuSiQue questions. The distilled models (Llama-8B, Qwen-7B) are separate architectures fine-tuned on R1 traces rather than true white-box compressed versions of the 671B model. The lower performance on MuSiQue likely reflects the well-known differences in pretraining data and parametric knowledge of the 7B/8B base models rather than an intrinsic property of distillation.

Limited novelty in finding final-layer sensitivity: In the broader model compression and mixed-precision literature, it is widely recognized that the first and last transformer layers (as well as specific MLP projections) are disproportionately sensitive to aggressive low-bit quantization, and keeping them at higher precision (16-bit or 8-bit) is a standard heuristic in practical deployment tools. Frame of this as an unexpected discovery specific to LRMs overlooks substantial prior work in general LLM quantization.

Heuristic and ad-hoc interpretability methodology: In Section 2.3, the authors state that 'we set all increases in relative importance to zero' because any increase compensates for decreases elsewhere. Manually zeroing out increases distorts the attribution shift distribution and undermines the causal interpretation. Furthermore, the identification of reasoning behaviors relies entirely on prompting GPT-4o without clear inter-annotator agreement metrics, validation, or ablation of prompt sensitivity.

Narrow validation of the proposed protection mechanism: The selective protection experiments in Table 4 are only evaluated on 3-bit AWQ on R1-Distill-Llama-8B. To substantiate the claim that this is a general solution across LRMs, experiments should include other architectures (e.g., Qwen models, 70B models) and other quantizers (e.g., GPTQ, GPTAQ).

Writing and presentation defects: The manuscript contains glaring drafting errors, including a truncated sentence in Footnote 1 ('Our interpretation code is a') and typos in prominent sections (e.g., 'imrpving' in Section 6).

strengths: Timely and practically significant research question investigating how compression (quantization, distillation, and pruning) affects the specialized reasoning behaviors of Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) like DeepSeek-R1.
Comprehensive empirical benchmarking covering multiple compression paradigms across multiple model families (Llama, Qwen, MoE R1) and diverse reasoning tasks.

Combines performance benchmarking with fine-grained mechanistic interpretability (difference of means and attribution patching) to causally pinpoint which components (e.g., final-layer MLP `up_proj` and `gate_proj`) are most critical for core reasoning behaviors.

Provides actionable and validated insights: selectively preserving final-layer MLP weights in higher precision (~2% of parameters) yields substantial accuracy recovery under challenging 3-bit quantization settings.
weaknesses: Small test sample sizes for several evaluation datasets (e.g., AIME 2024 has only 30 problems, and MuSiQue is evaluated on a sampled subset of 100 items), which can introduce variance and make fine-grained comparisons noisy.

The mechanistic interpretation depends on GPT-4o behavioral annotations over a relatively modest set of 120 instances, which, although checked for robustness in Appendix G, remains a heuristic proxy for identifying reasoning behaviors.

The finding that parameter count impacts parametric knowledge memorization more severely than reasoning capacity aligns closely with existing LLM scaling and compression literature, making that specific takeaway somewhat expected.

The mixed-precision validation (Table 4) is primarily demonstrated on R1-Distill-Llama-8B with AWQ; evaluating selective protection across more model scales and quantization frameworks (e.g., GPTAQ, Qwen architectures) would further solidify the empirical claim.

strengths: Timely and relevant topic: Investigating the effects of compression (quantization, distillation, and pruning) specifically on large reasoning models (LRMs) like DeepSeek-R1 and its distilled variants is an important and active area of research.

Bridges empirical benchmarking and mechanistic interpretability: Rather than merely measuring accuracy drops, the paper uses difference-of-means steering vectors and attribution patching across four specific reasoning behaviors (backtracking, uncertainty estimation, example testing, and adding knowledge) to localize compression sensitivity to specific weight matrices.

Actionable and validated insights: Locating the critical importance of the final-layer MLP (`mlp.up_proj` / `gate_proj`) leads directly to a simple, practical mixed-precision intervention (keeping the final layer in FP16), which yields a substantial gain (+6.57% average accuracy) for 3-bit AWQ.

Broad coverage of compression paradigms: The paper examines modern low-bit quantization (dynamic quantization, AWQ, GPTQ, GPTAQ, ANY4/3), pruning (SparseGPT, AlphaPruning), and distillation across both LLaMA and Qwen model families, with additional generalization checks on non-R1 models.
weaknesses: Small test set sizes on some benchmarks: AIME 2024 has only 30 problems, and MuSiQue is evaluated on a random subset of 100 questions. Given the small number of examples, single-digit differences in count translate to large percentage shifts, which can introduce variance into the quantitative comparisons.

Limited evaluation of the selective protection mechanism: The proposed mitigation (protecting the final-layer MLP modules in full precision) is only evaluated on 3-bit AWQ for R1-Distill-Llama-8B (Table 4). Demonstrating this intervention across multiple quantization techniques (e.g., GPTQ, GPTAQ) and across multiple model families/sizes (e.g., Qwen-7B/32B) would substantially strengthen the claim.

Small sample size for annotation validation: The behavior extraction relies on GPT-4o token annotation, which is validated with human agreement on only 10 sampled instances per behavior (Appendix G). The resulting 95% confidence interval for 'Adding Knowledge' includes negative correlation ([-0.218, 1.000]), indicating high estimation uncertainty in the human validation.

Evaluation metric for knowledge: Decoupling reasoning from knowledge retention primarily via 100 questions on closed-book MuSiQue is somewhat narrow for drawing overarching conclusions about general parametric knowledge retention versus reasoning ability.

strengths: Timely and relevant focus on understanding how compression techniques (quantization, pruning, distillation) specifically affect the reasoning dynamics of Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) such as DeepSeek-R1 and its distilled variants.

Bridges empirical benchmarking with mechanistic interpretability, employing difference-of-means steering vectors and attribution patching down to individual linear weight matrices (q, k, v, o, gate, up, down) rather than coarse layer-wise metrics.

Provides actionable insights and concrete empirical verification: demonstrating that final-layer MLP projections (notably mlp.up_proj) are disproportionately critical to reasoning behaviors, and showing that protecting just ~2% of weights in the final-layer MLP yields substantial gains (+6.57% average accuracy) for 3-bit quantization.
Thorough evaluation spanning multiple compression paradigms, model architectures (Llama, Qwen, and non-R1 models in Appendix J), bit-widths (1.58-bit to 4-bit), and sparsity levels.
weaknesses: Small sample sizes in parts of the empirical evaluation: MuSiQue evaluation is restricted to a random sample of 100 examples, AIME 2024 has only 30 questions, and the interpretability corpus relies on only 120 instances (30 per task), which may introduce variance.

The mechanistic analysis hinges on GPT-4o to automatically detect and tag reasoning behaviors (backtracking, uncertainty estimation, etc.). Although temperature consistency is checked in Appendix G, heuristic LLM labeling can introduce systematic label noise into the attribution patching gradients.

The claim that 'weight count has a greater impact on knowledge memorization than reasoning' relies heavily on closed-book MuSiQue performance compared to pure reasoning benchmarks, which partially conflates differences in task structure/evaluation metrics with parametric memory retention.

Comparison to existing mixed-precision and outlier-protection schemes (e.g., SpQR, OWQ, or OmniQuant layer-adaptive protection) is limited in Section 5.2, evaluating primarily against naive uniform 3-bit baselines.
